analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by all law enforcement and lets victims sue.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 15 Democratic cosponsors and given a single subcommittee hearing, the bill to ban racial profiling never received a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited police and other law enforcement from using race, ethnicity, or national origin to decide whom to stop, search, question, or investigate, and it would have let individuals hurt by profiling go to court to force changes. Federal agencies would have had to adopt anti-profiling policies and collect data on stops, and state and local agencies would have had to certify they do the same to keep receiving major federal policing grants. It was introduced by Sen. Russell Feingold in June 2001, got one subcommittee hearing, and died in committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Racial and ethnic minorities subjected to traffic stops, pedestrian stops, frisks, searches, and immigration-related investigations based on appearance. The bill's own findings cite a 2001 DOJ study showing Black and Hispanic drivers were more likely to be searched but yielded contraband far less often than white drivers (8% and 10% versus 17%), and a GAO study finding Black women citizens were nine times more likely to be X-rayed by Customs with lower hit rates [S3]. All residents also gain from public stop data, independent complaint procedures, and annual DOJ reports on profiling nationwide [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minorities targeted by police stops and searches

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits racial profiling by every federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement agent, covering traffic stops, pedestrian stops, frisks, searches, and immigration-related workplace investigations.

Creates a right for individuals injured by profiling to sue for court-ordered changes; statistical disparities alone count as prima facie evidence of a violation, and prevailing plaintiffs can recover attorneys' and expert fees.
Requires federal law enforcement agencies to adopt anti-profiling policies, collect and submit stop data, set up independent complaint procedures, and discipline agents who profile.

Conditions major federal policing grants (Byrne Memorial programs, COPS, Local Law Enforcement Block Grants) on agencies certifying anti-profiling policies, and funds training, data systems, in-car video cameras, and early-warning systems, with a share reserved for small and rural agencies.
Requires the Attorney General to report to Congress annually on racial profiling nationwide and makes the collected data available to the public.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies would bear the cost of data collection systems, complaint handling, training, and discipline procedures, and would face civil suits; state and local governments could have federal grant money withheld until they certify compliance; taxpayers would fund the best-practice grants and annual DOJ reporting [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies, governments facing suits, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Would have imposed data-collection, complaint-system, reporting, and discipline requirements on thousands of federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies at once, with real administrative costs.

Would have let statistical disparities in routine enforcement alone serve as prima facie evidence of a violation, exposing agencies to lawsuits over enforcement patterns even where no officer intended to profile.

Ties existing federal grant money to compliance certifications and lets the Attorney General withhold funds from noncompliant agencies — a condition some state and local officials would object to as federal intrusion into local policing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are mostly administrative — data systems, complaint procedures, training — and the bill directs grant money toward paying for much of that technology. The heavier cost falls on agencies exposed to lawsuits under a disparate-impact standard that does not require proof of intent. Set against the bill's own findings that profiling rarely uncovers contraband, humiliates innocent people, and erodes trust in police, the public benefit of an enforceable national ban outweighs the costs; the main honest objection is the reach of the disparate-impact litigation standard rather than the goal itself [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee — its only progress was one subcommittee hearing in August 2001 — until the two-year Congress ended, and it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Russell Feingold introduced the bill on June 6, 2001, with eight original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Fifteen Senate Democrats in total signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.
On August 1, 2001, the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution held a hearing on the bill.
The committee never held a markup, never voted the bill out, and the full Senate never debated or voted on it before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies that would have faced new data-collection mandates, complaint systems, civil liability, and conditions on federal grants were better off because the bill never advanced. Everyday people subjected to profiling gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that avoided new mandates and lawsuits

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 6, 2001, and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution
for.what_they_did: Held the bill's only hearing, on August 1, 2001 (S.Hrg. 107-537).

against.name: Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: His committee never reported the bill; after referral, its only action was the August 2001 subcommittee hearing, and no markup or committee vote ever followed.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred to test a partisan split, but every one of the bill's 15 cosponsors was a Senate Democrat and no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would have required data collection, complaint systems, and officer discipline, and exposed departments to civil suits with attorneys' fees, while also offering federal grants for cameras, data systems, and training. Departments' interest in avoiding liability and outside scrutiny of stop data runs against the public's interest in accountability.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (Customs, DOJ components, immigration and customs enforcement)
industries.note: The bill's findings cite a GAO report that Customs selected Black women citizens for X-ray searches at nine times the rate of white women with lower contraband hit rates, and it would have required federal agencies to adopt policies, submit data, and face suits. Federal agencies' institutional interest lay in keeping those practices unexamined.
The bill authorizes grants for in-car video cameras, portable computer systems, early-warning software, and anti-profiling training, creating a funded market for these suppliers.
